claims.text: HTTP methods tell the web server what kind of action the client wants to perform, while status codes provide a standardized numeric reply showing what happened

evidence.quote: In the previous lecture we learned how HTTP methods such as get, post, put, patch and delete allow client to tell a server what action it want to perform.
This is where HTTP status code become important because these are the standard numeric response that a server send back to a client.
So HTTP status code is a three-digit number written by a server in response to a request made by a client.

claims.text: The HTTP GET method requests data from a specified resource

evidence.quote: * GET: Requests data from a specified resource.

claims.text: An HTTP method is safe if it does not change server state

evidence.quote: A request method is safe if a request with that method has no intended effect on the server.

claims.text: A method is idempotent if making multiple identical requests has the same effect on the server as making a single request

evidence.quote: A request method is idempotent if multiple identical requests with that method have the same effect as a single such request.

claims.text: GET is both safe and idempotent

evidence.quote: | `GET` | Yes | Yes | Yes |

claims.text: GET can still send data to the server

evidence.quote: | GET | Retrieves data | URL (query parameters) | ❌ No | Read/fetch data |

claims.text: It does this by attaching query parameters directly to the request URL

evidence.quote: GET requests append data to the URL as query parameters (?name=value&role=admin), while POST requests send data in the request body.

claims.text: A query parameter is a key-value pair appended after a question mark in the URL string, such as /map?city=boston

evidence.quote: A query string can be appended to the path for additional information (usually in `key=value` format).
GET requests append data to the URL as query parameters (?name=value&role=admin)

claims.note: The passages support that query parameters are key-value pairs appended after a question mark in the URL, but the specific example `/map?city=boston` is not explicitly stated in the text.
claims.corrected_text: A query parameter is a key-value pair appended after a question mark in the URL string, such as ?name=value

claims.text: URLs have length limits that restrict GET requests to roughly 2,000 to 8,000 characters depending on the browser, and they can only transmit URL-safe text

evidence.quote: URL length limits restrict GET requests to roughly 2,000-8,000 characters, depending on the browser.
GET can only transmit URL-safe text, while POST can send any data type specified by the Content-Type header, such as JSON, XML, or binary files.

claims.text: Because GET requests are safe and read-only, browsers and intermediate proxies can cache them to speed up subsequent visits

evidence.quote: Since GET requests don’t modify data, browsers and proxies can safely cache responses to improve performance.

claims.text: The HTTP POST method submits data to be processed by a specified resource, such as creating a new database record or submitting an order form

evidence.quote: POST: Submits data to be processed to a specified resource.
The HTTP POST method submits data to a server to create a new resource or trigger an action.

claims.text: Unlike GET, POST sends its data inside the request body rather than the URL

evidence.quote: GET requests append data to the URL as query parameters (?name=value&role=admin), while POST requests send data in the request body.
Unlike GET requests, POST requests include a request body with the sent data and the ability to change the server state.

claims.text: A request body, or payload, is the data package sent directly after the HTTP headers

evidence.quote: Request Headers: Additional information about the request, such as browser details or accepted content types. * Request Body: Optional data sent to the server, commonly when submitting forms.

claims.note: The passages state that the request body contains optional data sent to the server, but do not specifically state it is sent 'directly after the HTTP headers' (though headers come before the body as per S5.p7).
claims.corrected_text: A request body is optional data sent to the server, commonly when submitting forms.

claims.text: POST can transmit any data format defined by the Content-Type header, including JSON, XML, or binary files, and it does not have the strict character length limits of URL query strings

evidence.quote: GET can only transmit URL-safe text, while POST can send any data type specified by the Content-Type header, such as JSON, XML, or binary files.
URL length limits restrict GET requests to roughly 2,000-8,000 characters, depending on the browser. POST has no such restriction and can handle megabytes of data.

claims.text: POST is not safe because it alters server state

evidence.quote: POST : The `POST` method submits an entity to the specified resource, often causing a change in state or side effects on the server.
In contrast, the methods POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, and PATCH are not safe. They may modify the state of the server or have other effects such as sending an email.

claims.text: POST is also non-idempotent: sending the same POST request multiple times will execute the operation multiple times

evidence.quote: The POST method is not idempotent, so sending the same POST request twice may create duplicate entries.

In contrast, the methods POST, CONNECT, and PATCH are not necessarily idempotent, and therefore sending an identical POST request multiple times may further modify the state of the server or have further effects, such as sending multiple emails.

claims.note: S15.p29 states that POST is 'not necessarily idempotent' rather than strictly non-idempotent in all absolute interpretations, though S11 and S2 categorize it as not idempotent.
claims.corrected_text: POST is not necessarily idempotent, so sending the same POST request multiple times may further modify the state of the server.

claims.text: For this reason, POST requests are not cached by default

evidence.quote: POST requests typically aren’t cached because they usually trigger actions or modify resources.
* POST requests are never cached

claims.text: Because GET puts parameters into the URL, sensitive parameters such as passwords or access tokens are visible on screen, saved in browser history, and recorded in server logs

evidence.quote: Because GET data lives in the URL, it appears in browser history, bookmarks, and server logs.
This exposes credentials in browser history, server logs, proxy logs, and referrer headers.

claims.note: The passages state that data in the URL appears in browser history and server logs, but do not explicitly mention being 'visible on screen'.
claims.corrected_text: Because GET puts parameters into the URL, sensitive parameters such as passwords or access tokens are visible in browser history and server logs.

claims.text: Moving data from the URL to the request body only hides it from the browser address bar and history

evidence.quote: POST data stays hidden in the request body, so you can’t bookmark it, but you also won’t accidentally leak credentials.

claims.note: The passages mention that POST data stays hidden in the request body, preventing bookmarks and accidental credential leaks, but do not explicitly state it only hides data from the browser address bar and history.
claims.corrected_text: Moving data from the request body hides it from being bookmarked or accidentally leaked.

claims.text: Plain HTTP sends both query strings and request bodies across the network unencrypted

evidence.quote: In HTTP implementations, TCP/IP connections are used using well-known ports (typically port 80 if the connection is unencrypted or port 443 if the connection is encrypted, see also List of TCP and UDP port numbers).

claims.note: The passages state that port 80 is used if the connection is unencrypted, but do not specifically mention query strings and request bodies being sent unencrypted over plain HTTP in that exact phrasing.
claims.corrected_text: Plain HTTP uses unencrypted connections across the network.

claims.text: An HTTP response begins with a three-digit status code issued by the server to tell the client the result of its request

evidence.quote: So HTTP status code is a three-digit number written by a server in response to a request made by a client.
* HTTP Status Code: Indicates whether the request was successful.

claims.text: Status codes are organized into five families based on their first digit

evidence.quote: These codes are divided into five categories: ### 1xx: Informational
So as you all know that HTTP status codes are grouped into five major categories. The first digit of the code tell us the category to which the response belongs.

claims.text: The 2xx class indicates that the client request was successfully received, understood, and accepted by the server

evidence.quote: 2XX successful The request was successfully received, understood, and accepted.
A success status indicates that the action requested by the client was received, understood, and accepted.

claims.text: When a read operation succeeds, the server usually replies with 200 OK and supplies the requested entity in the response body

evidence.quote: 200 OK Standard response for successful HTTP requests. The actual response will depend on the request method used. In a GET request, the response will contain an entity corresponding to the requested resource.

claims.text: When a request creates a new item on the server, such as a newly inserted user account, the server returns 201 Created

evidence.quote: 201 Created is another thumbs up, for when something new was created.

The server responds with details about the newly created resource: 
```
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /api/users/12345
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "id": "12345",
  "name": "Penny Ostman",
  "email": "[email protected]"
}
```

claims.text: The 4xx class indicates that the request cannot be fulfilled due to a problem on the client side

evidence.quote: 4XX client error The request cannot be fulfilled due to an issue that the client might be able to control.

claims.text: 404 Not Found means the requested URL resource does not exist on the server

evidence.quote: `404 Not Found` : The server cannot find the requested resource. In the browser, this means the URL is not recognized.

claims.text: The 5xx class indicates that the server encountered an internal failure while trying to process a request

evidence.quote: 5XX server error The server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request.
The HTTP `500 Internal Server Error` server error response status code indicates that the server encountered an unexpected condition that prevented it from fulfilling the request.
